qs.q: Which of the following is a unique characteristic of Parvovirus B19's genetic material compared to Adenovirus?
qs.e: Parvovirus B19 possesses single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), which is unique among the non-enveloped DNA viruses discussed. Adenoviruses, in contrast, have double-stranded DNA (dsDNA).
qs.s: Adenovirus & Parvovirus B19: Non-Enveloped DNA Virus Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Where does Adenovirus replicate within the host cell?
qs.e: Adenoviruses are DNA viruses that replicate within the host cell's nucleus. Parvovirus B19 also replicates in the nucleus, specifically in erythroid precursor cells.
qs.s: Adenovirus & Parvovirus B19: Non-Enveloped DNA Virus Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific serotypes of Adenovirus are responsible for causing Acute Respiratory Disease (ARD), characterized by fever, cough, and pharyngitis, particularly in close contact settings like military barracks?
qs.e: Serotypes 4 and 7 are associated with Acute Respiratory Disease and can be targeted with live oral vaccines in military recruits. Serotypes 40 through 42 are instead known to cause infant gastroenteritis.
qs.s: Adenovirus & Parvovirus B19: Non-Enveloped DNA Virus Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific adenovirus serotypes are recognized for causing infant diarrhea and account for approximately 15% of hospitalized cases of viral gastroenteritis in young children?
qs.e: Serotypes 40 to 42 are the specific strains responsible for viral gastroenteritis and infant diarrhea. Serotypes 4 and 7 are linked to respiratory illness rather than gastrointestinal disease.
qs.s: Adenovirus & Parvovirus B19: Non-Enveloped DNA Virus Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific structural component of the Adenovirus carries the viral attachment proteins and acts as a hemagglutinin?
qs.e: The fibers projecting from the adenovirus capsid carry the viral attachment proteins and exhibit hemagglutinating activity. Pentons carry type-specific antigens but do not serve as the primary attachment fibers.
qs.s: Adenovirus & Parvovirus B19: Non-Enveloped DNA Virus Guide: MCQs

qs.q: How does the typical duration of diarrhea caused by enteric adenovirus compare to that caused by rotavirus?
qs.e: Enteric adenovirus infections tend to be more prolonged, lasting 7 to 10 days, whereas rotavirus recovery generally occurs within 7 days.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Adenovirus is a non‑enveloped dsDNA virus that infects eyes, respiratory tract, gut and other organs. It causes self‑limited fever, cough, conjunctivitis and gastroenteritis, but can be severe in immunocompromised patients.

sections.p: Adenoviruses are icosahedral, non‑enveloped viruses with linear double‑stranded DNA. Over 50 serotypes exist, grouped into species A‑G, each with tissue tropism that guides clinical presentation.
b: Stable in the environment – survives drying and acid
Transmitted by droplets, fecal‑oral route, fomites, and water

sections.p: The virus enters cells via the coxsackie‑adenovirus receptor (CAR) and integrins, leading to lytic infection of epithelial cells. No viral envelope makes it resistant to disinfectants that target lipids.
b: Linear dsDNA ~36 kb
Non‑enveloped → resistant to desiccation
Serotypes A, C, D: respiratory; F: enteric

sections.p: Inhaled droplets cause respiratory disease; ingestion of contaminated water or food causes gastroenteritis; direct contact spreads conjunctivitis. After entry, viral replication occurs in the nucleus, producing new virions that are shed in secretions for 1‑2 weeks.
b: Incubation 2‑14 days
Shedding can continue after symptoms resolve

sections.p: Adenovirus produces a spectrum of illness: pharyngitis, bronchitis, pneumonia, conjunctivitis, and gastroenteritis. In children it is a leading cause of viral enteritis; in transplant or HIV patients it can cause severe, disseminated disease.
b: Respiratory: fever, cough, sore throat, possible lobar pneumonia
Ocular: pink eye, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis
GI: watery diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal cramps
Systemic: hepatitis, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis in immunocompromised

t.b: Does the patient have viral vs bacterial pneumonia? → Lobar infiltrates suggest bacterial; interstitial pattern supports viral adenovirus

t.a: PCR on respiratory or stool sample
t.b: Is adenovirus present? → Positive confirms diagnosis; negative does not rule out if sample unavailable
Has there been recent infection? → IgM rise supports acute infection; may be absent in immunocompromised

sections.p: Clinical suspicion is based on syndrome (e.g., conjunctivitis with fever) and epidemiology. Laboratory confirmation uses PCR or antigen detection from appropriate specimens. In low‑resource settings, rapid antigen tests or viral culture may be unavailable; diagnosis then relies on clinical pattern and exclusion of bacterial causes.
b: PCR is most sensitive and specific
Antigen detection useful for ocular specimens

sections.p: Supportive care is the mainstay: hydration, antipyretics, and oxygen if needed. Cidofovir or brincidofovir are reserved for severe disseminated disease in immunocompromised hosts. Infection control includes hand hygiene, surface disinfection with bleach, and isolation of affected patients.
b: No routine antivirals for mild disease
Cidofovir: inhibits viral DNA polymerase, used only in severe cases
Avoid routine steroids unless airway obstruction

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: adenovirus is a non‑enveloped dsDNA virus; it causes conjunctivitis, pharyngitis, and gastroenteritis; PCR is diagnostic; severe disease occurs in immunocompromised patients; control relies on hygiene, not antibiotics.
b: Most common viral cause of pediatric gastroenteritis after rotavirus
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis spreads via contaminated surfaces

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of meningitis or encephalitis (neck stiffness, altered mental status)
Persistent ocular pain or vision loss

faq.a: No; antibiotics do not affect viruses. They are only used if a bacterial superinfection is suspected.

faq.q: Why are outbreaks common in swimming pools?
faq.a: Adenovirus is resistant to chlorine at typical pool levels and can survive in contaminated water, leading to fecal‑oral spread.

faq.q: Is there a vaccine for adenovirus?
faq.a: Vaccines exist for military personnel against serotypes 4 and 7, but no routine civilian vaccine is available.
